takeaways: Minnesota had about 19,000 homes for sale in June (up 7.5% from a year earlier), the highest June inventory since 2019, according to the Minnesota Realtors figures Jason cites. It's a return toward normal, not an all-time high.
Buyers are keeping up: statewide new listings rose 11% and pending sales 8%. In the Twin Cities metro, inventory was almost 11,000 (up 5.1%), new listings up 10.5% and pending sales up 9.7%.
Buyers can again include inspection contingencies and ask for help with closing costs or repairs. Condos have cooled the most, with statewide condo sales down 2.7%.
It's not a free-for-all: metro homes averaged about 42 days on market (49 statewide), and metro sellers got about 99.6% of their original list price, before any concessions.
Homes listed from $250,000 to $350,000 are still the tightest part of the market, so well-priced starter homes can still draw multiple offers. Be pre-approved before you tour.
Prices held: the statewide median was $375,000 (up 1.4%) and the metro median $410,000 (up 2.1%). Statewide pending sales over $1 million rose 42%.
There were about 3.3 months of supply statewide and 2.8 in the metro. Jason argues today's balanced market is closer to 3 to 4 months than the traditional 5 to 6.
Sellers: price right from day one, fix the small things, and market well. Two weeks with little interest is the market telling you something.

faq.q: Is now a good time to buy a house in the Twin Cities?
faq.a: Buyers have more choice and negotiating room than at any point since 2019, with inspections and seller concessions back on the table. Well-priced homes, especially from $250,000 to $350,000, still sell fast, so get pre-approved first.

How long it would take to sell every home on the market at the current pace. In this video, the Twin Cities metro had about 2.8 months; Jason argues 3 to 4 months is roughly balanced in today's market.

takeaways: Minnesota gained about 8,300 more residents from other states than it lost in the latest year, its first net gain from domestic moves since 2018.

U-Haul's 2025 migration data, as cited, shows Wisconsin as the top origin state for one-way moves into Minneapolis, Chicago as the top origin metro, and California among the top 10 states for moves to Minnesota. Des Moines and Texas also send many movers.
Movers come for jobs at the region's Fortune 500 headquarters, a lower cost of living than the big coastal metros, four real seasons and Minnesota's lakes.
Minnesota has more miles of lake shoreline than California and Hawaii combined; Lake Minnetonka alone covers more than 14,000 acres.

Suburbs where many relocating buyers land, with prices as stated in the video (early 2026): Eden Prairie around the mid-$400,000s, Minnetonka in the low $500,000s (homes on Lake Minnetonka far higher), Bloomington in the mid to high $300,000s, and Plymouth from the high $400,000s.

Each suburb offers something different: Eden Prairie's parks and trails, Lake Minnetonka towns like Wayzata and Excelsior, Bloomington's airport access and the Mall of America, Plymouth's lakes and greenway, and Maple Grove's restaurants, Arbor Lakes and Elm Creek Park Reserve.

faq.a: Yes. In the latest year, Minnesota gained about 8,300 more people from other states than it lost, the first net gain from domestic migration since 2018.

faq.q: Where do most people moving to Minneapolis come from?
faq.a: According to the U-Haul data cited in the video, Wisconsin is the top origin state for one-way moves into Minneapolis and Chicago the top origin metro, with California, Iowa and Texas also sending many movers.

takeaways: Minnesota ranked first for quality of life in the State of the States report (the State of the Nation Project), which weighs 31 measures of work, health, civic and social life equally. Its average rank was 13.9, ahead of New Hampshire (14.6) and Iowa (15.9).
Minnesota didn't win any single category; it ranked near the top in almost all of them. U.S. News, using different methods, ranked Minnesota third.
Work drove the result: Minnesota ranked third for adults aged 25 to 54 who are working or looking for work, and third for the share with jobs.
The job base is spread across industries: 18 Fortune 500 headquarters, led by UnitedHealth Group, Target, Best Buy, 3M, U.S. Bank and General Mills, plus Mayo Clinic in Rochester.
Minnesota ranked fourth for social capital, volunteerism and low social isolation, and eighth for life expectancy.
Weak spots in the report: youth depression (43rd of 51), environment (32nd) and greenhouse gas emissions (38th).

Costs: as stated in the video, the statewide median sale price in July was $375,000 and the Twin Cities about $408,000, both under the national median. State income tax rates run from 5.35% to 9.85%, one of the highest top rates; clothing, groceries and prescriptions aren't subject to sales tax.

faq.q: Which state has the best quality of life?
faq.a: Minnesota ranked first in the State of the States report, which scores 31 measures equally. It didn't win any single category but placed near the top in almost all of them.

faq.q: How high are Minnesota's income taxes?
faq.a: Minnesota has four income tax brackets, from 5.35% to 9.85%. The top rate is one of the highest in the country, though it applies only to the top bracket.

takeaways: Minnesota's population passed 5.83 million in July 2025, adding about 33,000 people in a year: about 12,000 from births outnumbering deaths, about 12,500 from international moves and about 8,300 from other states.
That domestic gain is Minnesota's first since 2018. In the worst year, 2022, the state lost about 17,000 more people to other states than it gained.
People leaving often head to lower-tax or warmer states, with Florida gaining the most. People arriving come most often from Wisconsin, then North Dakota, Texas, California, Florida and Iowa.
Rural Minnesota is no longer shrinking overall: 46 counties outside the metro lost population in the 2010s, but only 19 did from 2020 to 2024.

Counties with a regional job hub kept growing: Olmsted (Rochester), Stearns (St. Cloud), Clay (Moorhead) and Blue Earth (Mankato). Wright County has grown fastest since 2020, while remote Traverse, Mahnomen and Kittson counties declined.
For buyers: ask how close a home is to a growing job center, whether the area depends on one employer, and whether there are enough nearby sales to compare when you sell.

faq.a: Yes. It passed 5.83 million in July 2025, adding about 33,000 people in a year from births, international moves and, for the first time since 2018, more people moving in from other states than leaving.

Counties with regional job hubs, such as Olmsted (Rochester), Stearns (St. Cloud), Clay (Moorhead) and Blue Earth (Mankato), plus Wright County, the fastest-growing since 2020, according to the video.

takeaways: Minneapolis itself isn't growing: about 430,000 people in 2020 and an estimated 428,500 in 2024. Hennepin County (1.27 million) looks steady because suburbs like Maple Grove, Rogers and Dayton are growing.

The growth is in the outer-ring counties: Scott (Shakopee, Prior Lake, Savage) up more than 20% since 2010, Carver (Chanhassen, Chaska, Waconia) up 25%, plus Dakota, Sherburne and Wright, which added more than 13,000 residents since 2020.

Why: Minneapolis and Saint Paul are largely built out, downtown office demand has shrunk (Target paid about $110 million to exit its City Center lease), and many buyers want yards and new construction.

Price ranges in the video: Lakeville from the mid-$400,000s, Chanhassen in the mid to high $500,000s, Shakopee and Apple Valley from the high $300,000s to mid-$400,000s, and Elk River and Big Lake from the low $300,000s.
Jason's advice: for long-term appreciation, buy where growth is heading. The trade-off is a 30- to 45-minute drive to downtown.

faq.q: Which Twin Cities counties are growing fastest?
faq.a: The outer-ring counties: Scott, Carver, Dakota, Sherburne and Wright. Carver is up about 25% and Scott more than 20% since 2010, according to the video.

takeaways: The National Association of Realtors reported in 2025 that the median age of first-time homebuyers hit a record 40.

The math as stated in the video: with a Twin Cities median of $375,000 (January 2026), 20% down is $75,000, plus $8,000 to $15,000 in closing costs. At 6% to 6.5%, principal and interest run about $2,000 a month, or roughly $2,600 to $2,700 with taxes and insurance.
NAR called the Twin Cities the most rate-sensitive housing market in the country: a one-point drop in rates would let about 81,000 more households here qualify to buy.
Three forces squeezed starter homes: owners holding 3% rates, investors buying entry-level homes as rentals from 2020 to 2023, and building costs too high to build homes under $300,000.
The frenzy has cooled: buyers can again negotiate, ask for rate buydowns and closing-cost help, and keep inspections.

What to do: know your full monthly cost, look at first-ring suburbs like Columbia Heights, Brooklyn Center, Robbinsdale, South St. Paul and Crystal, and check Minnesota Housing's first-time buyer and down payment programs at mnhousing.gov.

faq.q: How much do I need to buy a median-priced home in the Twin Cities?
faq.a: With the $375,000 median cited in the video, 20% down is $75,000 plus $8,000 to $15,000 in closing costs. Many first-time buyers put down less, and Minnesota Housing has down payment assistance programs.

faq.q: Is there down payment help for first-time buyers in Minnesota?
faq.a: Yes. Minnesota Housing (mnhousing.gov) offers first-time buyer loans and down payment assistance, with income and price limits. Check the current amounts and rules before you shop.

faq.q: What are affordable suburbs near Minneapolis?
faq.a: Jason suggests first-ring suburbs such as Columbia Heights, Brooklyn Center, Robbinsdale, South St. Paul and Crystal, which have lower prices than the most popular city neighborhoods.
